summary: Describes the architecture of the Internet Relay Chat (IRC) protocol and the roles of its components such as clients, servers and channels. Other documents give the detailed protocol rules. It is an informational memo.

eli5.summary: A big chat network is made of many connected rooms and helpers. This is the map showing what each piece does and how they fit together.

questions: how does internet relay chat work
why does irc use a spanning tree
subtitle: The map of Internet Relay Chat: servers joined in a tree, clients on the edges, and how messages travel.

tldr.problem: IRC had been documented in RFC 1459 and had kept evolving, so its architecture and the roles of its components needed an updated description.
tldr.mechanism: An IRC network is a group of servers connected as a spanning tree. Clients connect to servers, which register labels, host channels and relay every message, since clients never talk directly.
tldr.outcome: The memo also lists architectural problems: scaling, reliability, congestion and privacy. It updates RFC 1459 and points to separate documents for the detailed protocols.

today: RFC 2810 is an Informational memo that updates RFC 1459. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates RFC 2810 itself.

sections.title: Introduction and Components
sections.content:
The Internet Relay Chat (IRC) protocol is for text based conferencing. It was developed from 1989, originally so that users on a BBS could chat, and was first formally documented in May 1993 by RFC 1459. RFC 2810 updates that and describes the architecture of the current protocol, while other documents give the detailed protocol rules.

IRC uses the client-server model. The server is the backbone: the only component that can link the others together, giving clients and other servers a point to connect to. A client is anything connecting to a server that is not another server. User clients are programs with a text interface for interactive chat. Service clients are automatons, not meant for talking, with more limited access to chat functions and optional access to more private data from servers; the RFC's example is a service collecting statistics about the origin of connected users.

The memo says the distributed model, in which every server holds a copy of the global state, is still the protocol's most flagrant problem because it limits how large a network can grow.
sections.eli5: Servers are the post offices and clients are the people using them. Some clients are people chatting, and some are robots that do a job.

sections.title: A Spanning Tree of Servers
sections.content:
An IRC network is a group of servers connected to each other, and a single server is the simplest network. The only configuration allowed for servers is a spanning tree, where each server acts as a central node for the rest of the network it sees. Figure 1 in the RFC shows servers A to E with clients 1 to 4 hanging off them.

The protocol offers no way for two clients to talk directly. All client communication is relayed by the servers. The protocol provides three services: a client locator (a client registers a label on connecting, and servers track all labels in use), message relaying, and channel hosting and management. A channel is a named group of one or more users who all receive messages sent to it, and servers host channels and track their members.
sections.eli5: The servers are linked like branches of a tree with no loops, so there is exactly one road between any two. Every message travels along those roads.

sections.title: How Messages Are Delivered
sections.content:
For one-to-one messages, every server MUST be able to send a message in exactly one direction along the spanning tree to reach any client, so the path is the shortest path between two points on the tree. In Figure 1, a message from client 1 to client 3 is seen only by servers A and B and client 3.

For one-to-many, a channel plays the role of a multicast group. Conversation on a channel MUST only go to servers supporting users on that channel, and a message SHALL be sent only once over each local link, with each server fanning it out. Host or server mask messages go to users matching the mask, only to locations where such users are. Sending to a list of targets is the least efficient style, because the server dispatches a separate copy to each destination without checking for duplicates.

One-to-all messages are broadcasts. No message from a client results in a message to every other client. But most commands that change state, such as channel membership, channel mode or user status, MUST be sent to all servers by default, and the client cannot change that. Nearly all messages originating from a server are broadcast to the other servers.
sections.eli5: A note to one friend goes along the shortest road. A note to a room goes only to the post offices that have people in that room, and each office makes the copies for its own people.

sections.title: Known Architectural Problems
sections.content:
The RFC lists four problems that come from the architecture itself.

  • Scalability: the protocol does not scale well in a large arena, because all servers must know about all other servers, clients and channels, and updates must be spread as soon as anything changes.
  • Reliability: since the tree is the only allowed layout, every server-to-server link is a serious point of failure.
  • Network congestion: the architecture is extremely vulnerable to congestion. A failed link produces more traffic, and reconnecting servers, possibly elsewhere, produces still more. Servers are strongly RECOMMENDED not to reconnect automatically too fast.
  • Privacy: because servers must know everything about other entities, privacy is a concern, especially for channels, where the information reveals more than whether a user is online.
sections.eli5: Because every post office has to know about everyone, a bigger town gets harder to run. And if one road breaks, the whole town can get busy and confused.

sections.title: Security and Where to Go Next
sections.content:
The Security Considerations section says that, aside from the privacy concerns noted above, security is believed to be irrelevant to this document.

The detailed protocols are in companion documents: Client Protocol (RFC 2812), Server Protocol (RFC 2813) and Channel Management (RFC 2811). The RFC also lists mailing lists, software sources and the alt.irc newsgroup as places for discussion and implementations.
sections.eli5: This map does not talk about locks. For the exact rules of chatting, you read the companion guides.
